title: The stranger in your land
hookLine: a law with a memory attached: love the stranger, for you were strangers (Leviticus 19:34)
last: ONE BLOOD, EVERY FACE GOD'S IMAGE.

lines: A LAW WITH A MEMORY ATTACHED.
cards: The first week somewhere new has its own small terrors. Which door is the real front door. Which line you're supposed to stand in.
Whether that joke was friendly or not. Nobody tells you, and everyone else seems to know. Leviticus 19 is full of practical laws: pay your hired worker before morning, keep your scales honest.
And near the end of it sits a law about exactly that person, the one who doesn't know where the front door is. It comes with a reason attached, and the reason is a memory.

teach.b: This path met the stranger early, in Exodus, back on day three hundred ninety-six. The Hebrew word is ger: someone living among a people not their own, settled in, but not from here.

The law about the ger in Leviticus 19 reads, in the King James Bible: "the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt."
Notice the words as thyself. They echo a line from earlier in the same chapter, love thy neighbor as thyself. The stranger gets the same love as the neighbor, not a lesser version.
Then the reason. Not because strangers are useful, or because it's polite. Because you remember.

teach.h: YOU KNOW THE HEART OF A STRANGER.
teach.b: Exodus says it plainly: "ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." You know what it's like.
Jewish neighbors read these laws first, as their own Torah, and Christians received them as scripture too. Jesus carries the thread further.

teach.h: I WAS A STRANGER, AND YE TOOK ME IN.
teach.b: In his picture of the last judgment in Matthew, the king says, "I was a stranger, and ye took me in." So, in this reading, the newcomer at the door may be closer to Christ than they look.
Christians disagree, sincerely, about immigration laws and borders, and this path won't settle those arguments.
But these texts speak to something smaller and harder: the actual person in front of you, who doesn't know where the front door is.

how: Christians practice this through church welcome teams, refugee and immigrant ministries, English classes and meals for newcomers, and through simple hospitality to new neighbors, often citing Leviticus 19:34 and Matthew 25:35.

games.q: what does “the stranger in your land” mean?
o: a foreign army camped inside a nation's borders
a traveler passing through who must be fed once
a newcomer living among you, to be loved as your own

p: living among a people not your own
ye know the heart of a stranger
I was a stranger, and ye took me in

s: the command to love the stranger first appears in the New Testament
it's in the Torah: Leviticus 19:34, "thou shalt love him as thyself."
the law gives a reason: you were strangers too
"for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." the reason is a memory.
Leviticus asks a lesser love for outsiders than for neighbors
the stranger is to be "as one born among you," loved "as thyself," the same words used for the neighbor.

games.q: you farm in ancient Israel. a foreign family settles at the edge of your village. they don't know the customs. what does the law in Leviticus 19 ask?
o: keep a polite distance; they aren't from here.
treat them as one born among you, and love them as yourself.
help them only once they've learned your ways.
games.why: the stranger "shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself." the reason given isn't usefulness. it's memory: you were strangers in Egypt.

practice: Go back to a time you were the stranger: a new school, a new job, a new country, a family gathering where you knew nobody, and remember how it felt, and who, if anyone, showed you where things were.
Then bring to mind someone who is new near you now: a neighbor who just moved in, a new coworker, a new face at church or school. If you pray, you can hold that person before God.

wordCard.voice: The stranger in your land. The ger, the newcomer who isn't from here, to be loved as one born among you, because you know what it's like to be new.

orig.note: Hebrew: a stranger or sojourner, someone living among a people not their own; the word in Leviticus 19:34.

carryVoice: Your line: love the stranger. You know the heart of a stranger too. Rest well.
